Just War Theory
JUST WAR THEE-uh-ree
noun phrase (Christian ethics)
The Christian-ethical tradition governing the moral conditions under which war may be justly waged. Roots in Augustine (City of God, Contra Faustum); systematized by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q. 40); refined through the Reformed-confessional and broader Christian tradition. Two principal divisions: jus ad bellum (justice in going to war) and jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war).

Biblical Definition

The Christian-ethical tradition governing the moral conditions under which war may be justly waged and justly conducted. The tradition has roots in Augustine, was systematized by Thomas Aquinas, and was refined through the Reformed-confessional and broader Christian tradition. The criteria divide into two parts. Jus ad bellum (justice in going to war): (1) just cause (defense against aggression, protection of the innocent, righting of grave wrong); (2) legitimate authority (the lawful magistrate, who alone bears the sword, Romans 13:4 — not private individuals or factions); (3) right intention (the restoration of justice and peace, not conquest, plunder, or revenge); (4) reasonable hope of success; (5) proportionality (the good achieved must outweigh the harm); (6) last resort (war undertaken only after lawful alternatives are exhausted). Jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war): (1) discrimination (combatants may be targeted; non-combatants may not be deliberately targeted); (2) proportionality (the force used must be proportionate to the legitimate military objective). The biblical foundation includes the magistrate's God-given sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:1-4), the OT laws of warfare (Deuteronomy 20), and the broader biblical distinction between lawful civil-magisterial use of the sword and unlawful private vengeance (Romans 12:19). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds just war theory as the substantive Christian-ethical framework, rejecting both naive pacifism (which abandons the innocent to the aggressor) and unrestrained militarism (which ignores the moral constraints on warfare).

Webster 1828 Definition

Christian-ethical tradition governing moral conditions for just war; Augustine and Aquinas; jus ad bellum (just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, proportionality, last resort) and jus in bello (discrimination, proportionality); rejects both naive pacifism and unrestrained militarism.

JUST WAR THEORY, n. phr. (Christian ethics) The tradition governing the moral conditions for just war. Roots in Augustine; systematized by Aquinas (Summa II-II q. 40). Jus ad bellum: just cause, legitimate authority (the magistrate who bears the sword, Romans 13:4), right intention, reasonable hope, proportionality, last resort. Jus in bello: discrimination (non-combatant immunity), proportionality. Biblical foundation: the magistrate's sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:1-4); OT laws of warfare (Deuteronomy 20); the distinction between lawful civil use of the sword and unlawful private vengeance (Romans 12:19). Rejects naive pacifism (abandons the innocent) and unrestrained militarism (ignores moral constraints).

Key Scripture

Romans 13:4 — "For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Deuteronomy 20:10-12 — "When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it... And if it will make no peace with thee, but will make war against thee, then thou shalt besiege it."

Luke 3:14 — "And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages."

Ecclesiastes 3:8 — "A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace."

Modern Corruption

Just war theory is the historic Christian-ethical framework; the principal contemporary contest is between naive pacifism (which abandons the innocent) and unrestrained militarism (which ignores moral constraints).

expand to see more

The just war tradition is the substantive Christian-ethical framework that the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds against two opposing errors. Naive Christian pacifism (the Anabaptist tradition; much of contemporary progressive evangelicalism) treats all use of lethal force as unchristian, which abandons the innocent to the aggressor and denies the magistrate's God-given sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:4). Unrestrained militarism (the nationalist-jingoist temptation) ignores the moral constraints on warfare — the requirements of just cause, right intention, proportionality, non-combatant immunity. The just war tradition threads between these: war is sometimes a tragic moral necessity (the defense of the innocent against aggression), but it is bound by substantive moral constraints. The Christian soldier may justly bear arms (Luke 3:14, John the Baptist does not command the soldiers to leave their profession); the Christian magistrate may justly wage defensive war; but both are bound by the substantive just-war constraints.

Hebrew Roots

Augustine; Aquinas Summa II-II q. 40; jus ad bellum and jus in bello; magistrate's sword (Romans 13:4).
